extracted.intended_audience: researchers of peer review and conference stakeholders (authors, reviewers, meta-reviewers, and organizers), particularly in AI/ML (ICLR/OpenReview) communities
extracted.subtask_description: Large-scale empirical analysis of ICLR 2017–2025 OpenReview logs to identify process-level determinants of conference paper acceptance and produce actionable guidelines for authors, reviewers, and meta-reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Disagreement / Score Variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Score variance (σ²_i) among reviewers is a central determinant: disagreement generally lowers acceptance probability, with effects varying by score group (negative correlation in High-Score and Borderline groups; positive correlation in Low-Score group where a few high ratings can raise acceptance chances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use variance checks to detect outlier dominance; meta-reviewers should balance quantitative signals (score variance) with qualitative cues. Statistical tests show negative correlation with acceptance in High/Borderline, and a positive correlation in Low-Score papers (i.e., disagreement can sometimes help low-average-score submissions when at least one reviewer is supportive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer confidence (individual ck and mean ¯ci) was examined, especially for Borderline papers (5 ≤ ¯ri ≤ 6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidence exhibited negligible differences between accepted and rejected borderline papers and does not meaningfully predict acceptance in Borderline cases; therefore confidence should not be overweighted in mediation decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Sentiment (Tone of Comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant sentiment of review comments (positive/neutral/negative) strongly correlates with acceptance, particularly in Borderline cases: Positive → modest boost (35.4% acceptance), Neutral → baseline (32.6%), Negative → sharp reduction (18.8%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat negative sentiment as a strong constraining signal but separate tone from evidence; meta-reviewers should distinguish substantive criticisms from rhetorical negativity to avoid undue rejection based on tone alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal Response Speed (Latency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean latency of author responses (¯Ti) within the rebuttal window: faster responses (lower ¯Ti) are significantly associated with higher acceptance rates for Low-Score and Borderline-Score papers, but not for High-Score papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors of at-risk papers should reply promptly within the allowed rebuttal period (typically 7–14 days); promptness acts as a persuasive, rescue signal for Low/Borderline submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal Response Length (Substantiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean response length (¯Li): longer, substantive rebuttals increase acceptance likelihood for Low-Score and Borderline papers; little or no effect for High-Score papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide substantive, thorough rebuttals when scores are low or borderline; however, avoid verbose or unfocused replies that could be perceived negatively—content should be targeted and evidence-backed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction Depth and Response Count
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth (maximum depth of reviewer–author dialogue trees) and total number of author responses (Ni) matter: for Low-Score papers, more responses/depth consistently increase acceptance; for Borderline papers, moderate exchanges help but excessive depth can backfire; for High-Score papers, greater depth and counts correlate with declining acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an effective interaction window: dialogue depth of about 2–3 exchanges and a moderate number of responses tends to maximize acceptance prospects; avoid prolonged back-and-forth that may be seen as argumentative or inefficient, especially for already-strong papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing relative to the deadline (days before deadline) is predictive: early submissions (≥ 7 days before deadline) show higher acceptance rates (~44% vs overall ~38.9%), higher average reviewer scores, and lower reviewer disagreement (lower Gini index).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting earlier is an actionable strategy to improve acceptance odds—early submission correlates with stronger evaluations and more consistent reviewer judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: arXiv Posting and Posting Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and timing of arXiv postings affect acceptance: papers posted on arXiv outperform non-posted papers; posting simultaneously with or after submission (≤ 0h) yields ~6.4 percentage points higher acceptance than earlier preprints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate arXiv posting with submission (synchronized or immediate post-submission posting) to signal readiness and completeness; posting can function as an informative external signal even under double-blind review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility Supporting Resources (Code/Data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing reproducibility resources (supplementary material, code, data — 'with-RS') strongly predicts higher acceptance (with-RS acceptance ≈ 43.96% vs without-RS ≈ 32.54%; logistic OR ~1.626).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include code, data, and other reproducibility artifacts when possible; meta-reviewers and organizers are encouraged to explicitly reward reproducibility and link credits to validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Elements: Tables, Figures, Equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of visual elements relate to novelty and contribution: tables and equations correlate positively with empirical contribution and contribution scores; excessive visuals may lower perceived technical novelty; figures tend to boost empirical novelty but may negatively correlate with technical novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design visuals according to the paper’s goals: use concise visuals to highlight technical novelty and use more tables/figures/equations to strengthen empirical persuasiveness and contribution. Cap and curate visuals to avoid signaling lack of technical novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: English Fluency, Clarity, and Linguistic Style
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic metrics (vocabulary diversity, average sentence length, Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch–Kincaid Grade, Gunning Fog Index) correlate with acceptance, and relationships shifted after widespread LLM use: pre-LLM (2017–2023) easier-to-read writing and slightly longer sentences were modestly advantageous; post-LLM (2024–2025) reviewers favored 'professional, somewhat difficult tone' combined with short/concise sentences ('Professional but concise').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clear, targeted, and evidence-backed language; adapt style to the present context (post-LLM preference for concise professional tone). Avoid excessive vocabulary diversity or unreadable prose; short, dense, professional sentences are effective in the post-LLM era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference Recency
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference recency metrics (average reference age, recent references ratio, old references ratio) influence empirical novelty: older references decrease empirical novelty while a higher recent references ratio increases it; technical novelty is largely unaffected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite recent relevant work to boost perceived empirical novelty; a high fraction of recent references signals engagement with the latest literature and supports novelty assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score Group Definitions and Tailored Strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers are grouped by mean reviewer score ¯ri into High-Score (¯ri > 6), Borderline (5 ≤ ¯ri ≤ 6), and Low-Score (¯ri < 5); recommended tactics differ by group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor rebuttal and submission strategies by score group: Low (<5) — respond quickly and substantively, keep depth 2–3, provide RS, write concisely with supporting tables/equations; Borderline (5–6) — balance speed and substance, counter negative sentiment with precise clarifications, use early submission and synchronized arXiv posting, emphasize recent references; High (>6) — avoid excessive interactions, consolidate contributions and provide RS and concise conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-reviewer & Organizer Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations for meta-reviewers and organizers include applying variance checks to prevent outlier dominance, managing interactions by encouraging 2–3 dialogue turns while treating longer debates with caution, separating evidence from tone to buffer undue negativity, and explicitly rewarding reproducibility resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-reviewers should weigh quantitative indicators (scores, variance) together with qualitative cues (sentiment, rebuttal content), encourage efficient rebuttal windows (optimal depth ~2–3), avoid letting negative tone override evidence, and implement policies to credit reproducibility artifacts to improve fairness and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Interaction Window (Optimal Rebuttal Activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an effective range for rebuttal activity: an optimal dialogue depth of around 2–3 exchanges and a moderate number of responses tend to maximize acceptance prospects; beyond that, diminishing or negative returns emerge, especially for High-Score papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should aim for focused rebuttals with limited iterative exchanges; meta-reviewers should discourage protracted debates and encourage concise, evidence-focused clarifications.
